courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Introduction to the Hebrew Bible
courses.description: This course is a survey of the books which made up the Hebrew Scriptures, and the lives of the people whom these books are about. It covers the period of the Patriarchs to the beginning of the Christian era within the context of the ancient Near Eastern world. This historical survey will also introduce students to the life and faith and literature of the Hebrew people. During the course, students are expected to read and become familiar with the Hebrew Scripture.
courses.course_syllabus:
Topics (Key concepts)

Introduction (Imaginative Remembering; Genre)

Torah, Genesis; (Myth, Legend and ANET)

Exodus, Leviticus; (Cult and Priestly school)

Numbers, Deuteronomy; (Law and Narrative)

Prophets, Joshua, Judges; (History and Deuteronomistic History)

1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings; (Prophet in Narrative)

Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel; (Literary Prophet and Their Social World)

Minor Prophets; (Twelve prophet as a book)

Writings, Psalms; (Poetry as Torah)

Job; Proverbs (Wisdom Literature)

Five Scrolls; (Hebrew Bible and the early Judaism)

Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, (2nd Temple Literature)

1 and 2 Chronicles; (The Rewritten Bible)

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Introduction to the New Testament
courses.description: This course is a survey of the New Testament Church, its life, faith and literature within the context of the Mediterranean world. During the course, students are expected to read and become familiar with the contents of the New Testament.
courses.learning_outcomes:
A) Knowledge Outcome:

- To give students a general understanding of the text of the New Testament, its methods of studies, its background and the issues involved.

B) Attitude Outcomes:

- To develop students’ appreciation of the New Testament text as well as the diversity of interpretation of it.

- To develop students’ ability to have a critical, yet sympathetic understanding of the New Testament.

- To develop students’ analytical mind in reading scholarly opinions.
courses.course_syllabus:

Course Requirements, Tools, Text; Methods of Biblical Studies; Manuscript & Translation

Sessions 2-3:

Pauline Epistles/Letters: Characteristics & Authenticity Paul & his Mission

Sessions 4-6:

Synoptic Gospels: Text, Synoptic Problem, Two-source Theory, Form & Redaction Criticism, Recent Trends

Sessions 7-8:

Johannine Literature: Structure, Source Date & Place Authorship, Catholic Epistles

Session 9:

Social Context of the New Testament

Sessions 10-11:

Jesus of History: Survey Jesus of Nazareth Jesus’ Traditions Sources

Session 12:

Canon & Canonization, Authority of the Bible

Session 13:

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Prophetic Literature
courses.description: Exegesis of selected passages from Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve Prophets.
courses.course_syllabus:
Major concepts and topics to be covered:

1. The social world of the Hebrew prophets

This section covers the role of a prophet and the nature of prophecy in ancient Southwest Asia and Israel in relation to the social issues of its time.

2. The historical context

The Hebrew prophets will be situated in their signifying contexts from the Neo-Assyrian empire to the Persian empire.

3. Major sections and Individual books

The structure and literary features of prophetic literature of different major sections (the Former Prophets, the Latter Prophets, and the Twelve) and individual books will be adumbrated.

4. Critical approaches

Recent scholarship in a variety of critical methods will be discussed.

5. Theological notions

Major theological notions include covenant, messianism, inviolability of Zion, theodicy, retributive logic, universalism, ḥesed, and restoration.

6. Critical Issues

Critical issues include vaticinium ex eventu, the scheme of prophecy and fulfillment, social justice, the marital and sexual metaphor, divine violence, and historicity.

Course schedule:

Session 1:

Introduction to Prophetic Literature

Session 2:

The Social and Historical Context of the Hebrew Prophets

Session 3:

- What was a prophet?

- What was prophecy?

- Prophets and institutions

- Vaticinium ex eventu

Session 4:

- Prophetic genres

- Critical approaches and reading strategies

Session 5:

- Navi’im: The Former Prophets, the Latter Prophets, and the Twelve

- Female prophets

Session 6:

- The eighth-century prophets: Amos, Hosea, Micah, Proto-Isaiah

- Social critiques

Session 7:

- The late seventh-century minor prophets: Nahum, Zephaniah, Habakkuk, Obadiah

- Divine violence

Session 8:

- The early sixth-century Prophets: Jeremiah

Session 9:

- The early sixth-Century prophets: Ezekiel

- Marital and sexual metaphors

Session 10:

- Class Excursion: Poverty in Hong Kong

Session 11:

- The Persian prophets: Deutero-Isaiah and Trito-Isaiah

- Excursion debriefing

- Presentation of term-paper abstract

Session 12:

- The Persian prophets: Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Joel

Session 13:

- The fictional prophet: Jonah Concluding remarks

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Synoptic Gospels
courses.description: This course comprises a study of the synoptic problem, the characteristics, purpose and theology of the three Synoptic Gospels, and a detailed exegesis of selected passages from the Gospels both of Matthew and of Luke, including comparison with parallel passages in the Gospel according to Mark.
courses.learning_outcomes:
A) Knowledge Outcome:

- To give students a general understanding the text of the Synoptic Gospels, the methods of studies and the issues involved.

B) Attitude Outcomes:

- To develop students’ appreciation of the Synoptic Gospels as well as the diversity of their interpretation.

- To develop students’ ability to have a critical, yet sympathetic understanding of the text.
courses.course_syllabus:
Session 1:

Session 2:

Session 3:

Session 4:

Session 6:

- Messianic Secret 2

Session 8:

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Pauline Letters
courses.description: Study of selected passages from Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, Ephesians, Philippians and Colossians, including general questions of date, authorship, setting, purpose and main theological emphasis.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:

- To have the overview on the interpretation history of Pauline letters and their emphasis, development and trend.

- To have an overview on the key concepts and theological motifs of Pauline letters.

Skill Outcome:

- To be equipped with the necessary interpretation skills, based on the socio-rhetorical interpretation, to develop their own interpretation on Pauline letters.
courses.course_syllabus:
I) List of Topics

1. Problem in interpreting Pauline Letters

Learning the complication of interpreting Paul from historical and theological perspectives.

2. Basic concepts in interpreting Pauline Letters

Introducing various basic concepts in interpreting Paul including who Paul was, the context of Paul and the language Paul used, etc.

3. Interpretation History of Pauline Letters

Learning the development and differences in concerns and assumptions of various main stream interpretations beginning from the reformation.

4. Pauline Theological motifs

Learning the key theological motifs scholars generated from the undisputed Pauline letters.

5. Socio-rhetorical interpretation (SI)

Learning the methodology of SI and how it could help us to bring the economic “texture” into biblical exegesis.

6. Detail analysis of selected passages from Romans, Philemon and Philippians

Selected passages will be analyzed using the method and concepts introduced in the course

II) Course Schedule

Session 1:

Course Introduction + Problems in interpreting Paul

Session 2:

Basic concept in interpreting Pauline letters

Session 3:

Interpretation history of Pauline letters

Session 4:

Context of Paul (1): 2nd temple Judaism and New Perspective of Paul

Session 5:

Context of Paul (2): Social World of Paul including the Political and Economic situation of Roman Empire

Session 6:

Core Pauline theological motif 1 - Theology

Session 7:

Core Pauline theological motif 2 – Eschatology

Session 8:

Core Pauline theological motif 3 - Christology

Session 9:

Core Pauline theological motif 4 - Love

Session 10:

Interpretation Method: Socio-rhetorical Interpretation 2

Session 11:

Letter to Philemon: Demonstration of SRI application

Session 12:

Conclusion

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Early and Medieval Church
courses.description: The purpose of the course is to introduce the students to the historical and theological developments in the early and medieval church, from Jesus to the 15th century. The course offers a general knowledge of the theological and ecclesial development during the covered period and helps students get acquainted with different perspectives on church history and with issues that are still debated.
courses.learning_outcomes: The students will gain a general knowledge of the theological and ecclesial development during the covered period and get acquainted with different perspectives on church history and with issues that are still debated. The students will also develop sensitivity regarding the diversity of Christian faith expressions.
courses.course_syllabus:
Session 1 - The church in the first two centuries

Session 2 - Christianity and politics: Conflicts with the State; the extension of Christianity in the first three centuries

Session 3 - Challenges to the Faith in the Second Century and the Development of Early Catholic Theology

Session 4 - Christianity and culture: The encounter with Hellenist philosophy and the development of Patristic theology

Session 5 - Christianity becoming the religion of the empire: Constantine and his impact on the religious life of the Catholic Church

Session 6 - Theological and ecclesial controversies of the 4th Century: Donatism and Arianism

Session 7 - Theology and christological debates in the 5th century: The Council of Chalcedon; Augustine

Session 8 - Mission history in medieval times: the extension of Christianity and its inculturation in new contexts

Session 9 - Church and state: The growth of papal and ecclesial power through the middle ages and the conflict between emperor and

Session 10 - The history of a growing division: The churches in East and West on separate ways

Session 11 - The history of the other church: Revivalism, reform, and alternative Christian faith expression in the medieval time

Session 12 - Outward militancy and inward divisions in the high and late medieval time: the crusades, the inquisition and ecclesial divisions

Session 13 - A short introduction to medieval theology

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: The Reformation Era
courses.description: The development of Christian thought and institutions in the age of the Reformation.
courses.learning_outcomes:
a) The students will gain a general knowledge of the ecclesial and theological developments during the covered period.
b) The students will learn how the shifts in 16th century Europe affected later historical and theological developments.
c) Students will develop sensitivity regarding the diversity of Christian faith expressions.
courses.course_syllabus: The purpose of the course is to **introduce the students to the developments in church and theology in 16th century Europe**, a crucial period in the history of the church, as it brought unprecedented changes that can be described as a paradigm shift in Christianity. After the course the student shall be able to understand different aspects of the transformations happening during this period: theological, spiritual, historical, social, cultural, political, and others. A special emphasis will be on the shifts in theological thinking and how these shifts affected the traditional configuration of society, state, culture, and religion.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Humanity and Salvation
courses.description: The Christian doctrine of humanity; the doctrine of sin and its consequences; various concepts of salvation; the doctrines of reconciliation, justification, sanctification, etc.; Christ and salvation.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcomes

1. To understand Christian doctrine of human being and salvation.

2. To understand the key issues of the past and current discussion about these doctrines.

3. To be able to articulate answers to the current problems by using these Christian resources.

Attitude outcomes

1. To develop a critical yet constructive attitude in understanding the relationships between the Christian idea on human being and salvation.

2. To develop a sensitivity to the practical effectiveness of these doctrines.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Systematic Theology I
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the nature and methodologies of Christian theology, with particular attention to the historical creeds of the Christian Churches.
courses.learning_outcomes: After completing this course, the student is expected (a) to have a basic understanding of the history of Christian theology; (b) to understand the nature and roles of various factors that influences the formation of theology (especially the Bible, but also tradition, culture, theological language, etc.); (c) to have elementary knowledge of exemplary theological systems and methods; (d) to develop a basic competence in appreciating theological texts.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Pastoral Theology
courses.description: This course covers three areas: (1) the place of Pastoral Theology in theological studies and its uniqueness; (2) different types of Pastoral Theology and their aims; and (3) church models and pastoral emphases.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To understand what is Pastoral Theology with reflection from personal pastoral experience.

2. To construct Pastoral Theology from the Bible, church and Chinese cultural traditions.

3. To understand different emphases of Pastoral Theology from multiple perspectives and from histories of different denominations.
courses.course_syllabus:
課程綱要

一）何謂牧養神學？

二）牧者為中心的牧養神學
\*牧者的角色：牧人？羊？先知？祭司？領袖？僕人？教師？神學家？

\*牧者的功能與責任：餵養？照顧？宣講？ 禮儀？領導？行政？教導？輔導？探訪？ 佈道？栽培？訓練？社會活動？社會服務？

\*牧養範圍有何界線？

三）牧者與成長
\*牧者的危機

\*牧者成長的攔阻

四）信徒(需要)為中心的牧養神學

\*信徒需要些什麼？

\*對信徒有什麼期望？

五）信仰群體為中心的牧養神學
\*教會存在的意義與功能

\*教會的成長和發展

六）世界為中心的牧養神學
\*在世與不屬世

\*天國的使命

七）教會與發展
\*聖禮、崇拜

\*訓練與栽培

\*教會增長與植堂

八）世界與個人
\*社會、政治

\*生寄死歸

課節安排

第一節：牧者的角色

第二節：何謂牧養神學

第三節：牧者的本質、功能與責任、牧者為中心的牧養神學

第四節：牧者的能力、恩賜、靈性、心態和心理健康

第五節：讀書報告分享

第六節：個人牧養、生寄死歸

第七節：聖經中教會的諸形象、教會為中心 的牧養神學

第八節：使命為中心的牧養神學

第九節：植堂策略個案研討

第十節：教會領導、組織文化在教會群體中的協同效應與信徒運動的推展

第十一節：崇拜、聖禮、聖曆與牧養

第十二節：教會增長研討

第十三節：多元化的牧養神學、牧養神學的再思

4. Reflect and articulate how this Topic can be relevant in the various contexts.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: History of Christianity in Hong Kong
courses.description: This course aims at an in-depth study about the historical development of Christianity (including Protestant and Catholic churches) in Hong Kong since the beginning of the British rule. This study will emphasize the role of Christianity in the wider context of the history of Hong Kong, with special focus on the relationship between Christianity and Hong Kong society (education, medical care, social service, social action, etc.) and various issues arising from these areas.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To assist students to understand the history of Protestant Christianity in Hong Kong.

2. To assist students to acquaint the methods of conducting research on local church history.

3. To develop and affirm students’ identity towards local church history.
courses.course_syllabus:
一、導論：從大歷史看香港基督教
二、開基與拓荒：香港基督教的建立（1841 - 1860）

三、華南與香港：發展與自立（1860 - 1936）

四、難民與福音（1937 - 1960’s）

五、本土教會的形成（1970’s - ）

六、傳教與教育：香港教會辦學
七、天國與社會：基督教與社會參與
八、上帝與該撒：政教關係在香港
九、福音與文化：西洋、中華、本土的交融

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Homiletics

meetings.instructor:
Dr. LI Kwan Hung Leo, 
Professor YIP Ching Wah Francis

courses.description: This course will cover: (1) the principles, construction and technique in preaching; and (2) the content and message of a sermon in the contemporary world. Student’s preaching will be videotaped and discussed for improvement of technique and content.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To understand the principle of preaching on theological topics.

2. To understand the integration of different types of preaching and the way of preparation.

3. To learn and practice the techniques and styles in delivering a sermon.
courses.course_syllabus:
一、 課程評估
分享／引論
聽道／講道經驗及心得
何謂講道學（Homiletics）？

講道的構成因素——真道、表達、使命、講者、聽眾、技巧、權柄

二、 真道
何謂道？
聖經與道
宣講與教導之不同
道與行

三、講章的分類
專題式講道
經文式講道
釋經講道

四、講章的性質
佈道
培靈
奮興
牧養
婚禮
喪追思
紀念日
聖曆及特別主日

五、經文的選擇與運用
用一段經文的好處
選擇經文要留意的地方
如何運用經文

六、如何決定主旨
主旨的必要
主旨的選擇

七、如何決定題目

八、講章的結構
分段與大綱
引論、本論、結論

九、導言
三個目的

十、例證
講道的天窗

十一、結論與應用
應用的重要性
應用的三個成份
應用的動機

十二、講章的準備和組成的步驟
探索期
專注期
講章的組合
最後的準備

十三、講道的技巧
講者的素質與風格
講章的表達與演繹

十四、學生試講

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Preaching
courses.description:
Through instructions and discussion, students are given guidance in their composition and delivery of sermons. Special emphasis will be given to Biblical exposition, progression of thoughts, flow of feelings, use of illustrations, relevance, and delivery styles. Each student is expected to deliver a full-length sermon in front of other students two to three times a semester and hand in the relevant scripts at the same time.

Offerings with different subtitles can be taken up for credit, up to a maximum of two times.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Prerequisite: THEO3241.
courses.learning_outcomes: 本科目主要目的為鍛鍊講章的撰寫及宣講的技巧，特別著重聖經的闡釋、思路的發展、信息的凝聚、情感的表達、引寓的運用、處境的適切、宣道的風格及真道的應用。老師會就個別同學的表現提供批評指導，以改進同學講道的質素。
courses.course_syllabus:
第1節：

課程介紹；宣道者個人靈性、學養、性向與風格的關係

第2節：

既是宣講，也是做神學(Doing theology)：宣講、神學與處境之關聯

第3節：

觀摩與評論

第4節：

宣講微技巧

第5節：

講章類別的撰寫與演繹：釋經講道(Expository preaching)

第6節：

宣講與修辭技巧

第7節：

講章類別的撰寫與演繹：主題式講道(Topical preaching)

第8節：

講章類別的撰寫與演繹：處境講道(Situational preaching)

第9節：

講章類別的撰寫與演繹：敘事講道(Narrative preaching)

第10節：

講章類別的撰寫與演繹：佈道式講道(Evangelistic preaching)

第11節：

在危機中的宣講

第12節：

宣講與多媒體應用

第13節：

向不同群體的宣講方式

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Faculty Student Seminar I
courses.description: This course aims to develop practical research and academic writing skills of students. They are required to choose a subject for a paper, to create a logical structure, and to construct their own arguments academically. Their papers will be presented at the seminars. Chosen topics of the paper should be related to theological areas such as systematic theology, biblical studies, church history, practical theology, gender theology and so on. Nevertheless, students are encouraged to discuss current issues and subjects of other disciplines relating to the modern world from a theological perspective. Students’ performances will be primarily assessed by their written papers and presentations, but also by their participation in the discussion session. They will be evaluated on their ability to think theologically, that is, to reflect upon major theological and social issues, to define current issues in theological terms, and theological issues from the perspective of other disciplines.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes: This course will enhance students’ research skills, critical thinking and independent learning. The former will be achieved through the students’ own discovery of a subject that concerns academic interests and is feasible within the time and word limit, reviewing certain academic discussion of their chosen subjects, creating appropriate research methodologies, searching for and selecting materials, making sound judgements, engaging in meaningful dialogue with the newly-discovered information and former knowledge, and finally drawing up a sensible conclusion. This learning process is totally dependent on students’ own initiatives, creativity, sensitivity to theological and other issues, diligence, writing skills, as well as the awareness of self-limitations which can be reflected by their actively seeking advice from course instructors and through discussion with student peers. Students will be encouraged to move out of their own ‘comfort zones’ in order to critically evaluate new information and knowledge and apply this to the contemporary context.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. academic writing style
2. structure of academic papers
3. developing a good research topic & title
4. developing a thesis statement and defend it
5. how to write an Introduction
6. literature review and the ways to argue for a research gap/agenda
7. arguing theologically and reasonably
8. writing an abstract
9. Chicago-style citation
10. academic honesty
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

Mewburn, Inger, Katherine Firth, and Shaun Lehmann. How to Fix Your Academic Writing Trouble: A Practical Guide. London: Open University Press, 2018.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Graduate Project I
courses.description: Graduate project is a capstone for theological students in their final year to integrate their learning across theological disciplines through the completion of an action project. It is driven by the interests and experiences of the students. Under the supervision of a faculty member, the student proposes and completes a project with a critical and reflective theological evaluation of the practice of ministry in the Church and/or the society. In order to complete the capstone project, the student has to take THEO5009, 5010 and 5011 as a whole in his/her/hir final year.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.course_syllabus:
Graduate Project welcomes a variety of creative project proposals that aim to integrate the student's passions and raison d'etre with his/her/hir unique embodiment of text, spirituality, and culture. It could be an original, creative work of art that demonstrates Christian aesthetics or a practical theological project that addresses a specific issue in ministry, engaging in dialogue with relevant analyses of contemporary culture(s) and Christian tradition(s) (themes, symbols, community, literature, etc). Through Graduate Project, the student is expected to demonstrate his/her/hir ability to integrate academic, practical, and spiritual knowledge/understanding to address a real-world issue. In order to facilitate the learning process, culminating assignments are distributed throughout the academic year. The core syllabus includes the elements below:

1. Project Proposal Writing: Among other things, project objectives, rationale, time frames, delivery, intended outcomes, and evaluation methods.
2. Project Report: After completing the project, the student is required to submit a written report of approximately 5000 words that includes an evaluation of the project's goal achievement and suggestions for future improvements. Furthermore, the report must include a theological reflection on the project via a critical dialogue between Christian tradition(s), the student's own foundational theological assumptions, and the project context. The student is also required to submit project products or deliverables such as PowerPoint slides, educational resources, or video of an event, in addition to the written report, to demonstrate his/her/hir performance and creativity.
3. Presentation at a "Theology Salon": At the end of the academic year, students are invited to present their projects at the Theology Salon, where students and teachers engage in a critical theological discussion of the students' project accomplishments.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Women in World Missions
courses.description: In the context of Christianity as a worldwide movement, the majority of church members are women. Since the early 1800s, women have led in cross-cultural ministries of service, witness, evangelism, and philanthropic works. In order to understand these phenomena, this course will explore the context, nature, theory, and issues relating to women in world missions with particular focus on the 19th century to the present. In addition to examining important global issues for women in missions, it will cover women encounter with local culture through which to explore any selective appropriation of Western Christianity from intercultural perspective.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity or MA Christian Studies or MA Theological Studies
courses.learning_outcomes: Students will be able to identify and analyze some of the critical concepts, methods, and debates in women and World missions; to discover historical agencies of both two categories of women, i.e., non-Western women and women missionaries; and to become aware of any gender factors shaping our understandings of mission theologies and practices.
courses.course_syllabus:
Gendered Imperialist Mission and History of Global Mission as Women’s History

Women Missionary Movement in the World Missions

Multiple Allegiances of Women Missionaries

Multiple Agency of Native Women

Independent Evangelical Missions and Pentecostalism

The Ecumenical Women’s Missionary Movement

Roman Catholic Women in Missions

Cultural Collision in Women and Missions, i) Footbinding and Anti-Footbinding Movement, ii) Controversy of Female Circumcision in Africa, iii) Women and Caste System in India

Current Global Issues

Rethinking Feminist Missiology

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Theology and Feminism
courses.description: The absence of women’s experiences and voices often seems the result and perpetuation of a blindness to gender inequality within the Church. To change this reality, we must return to a basic question: What does Christian theology reveal to the Church about the nature and place of women? The course aims at exposing students to a broad perspective and discussion about the dynamic relationship between theology and feminism. In addition to introducing the experiences of contemporary women and feminist critiques on violence, family, sexuality, poverty, ecology and media, the students will be encouraged to reexamine the ways in which the Western Judeo-Christian religious tradition has profoundly influenced our understanding of God and gender and to study the feminist interpretations of God-talks, sin and redemption, spirituality, leadership and church.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity, MA in Theological Studies, MA in Christian Studies, MA in Religious Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Delineate the historical oppression of the female gender in Church History and the Judeo-Christian traditions.
2. Review and describe the theological history of women’s identity, status and role in the family, church and society at large.
3. Analyze and criticize how theologies are formulated against the female gender in Christian history until today. Evaluate how formulations of the God-talk and other aspects of theology are also influenced by such theologies. Comment and specify the abuse, violence, subversion and impoverishment of the female gender and their relation to ecology.
4. Research and reconstruct female presence in history and Christian sources.
5. Describe and explain what constitutes gender, sexuality, and female embodiment, and draw implications on these discourses in the academia.
6. Construct practical frameworks to educate and raise awareness of the oppression, and also propose ideas how to promote a just and righteous community of faith and society.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction: The Emergence of Christian Feminist Theology; FT as Intersectional Theology
2. The Construction of the Other
3. Workshop Brainstorming: Tell the OTHER Stories
4. Art Workshop (Full Day): I and the Other in God, Facilitated by Liu Kwok Hong
5. Feminist Theology as a History of Theology
6. Asian Feminist Theology and Post-Colonial Christology
7. Ecofeminist Theologies
8. Open Ceremony of the Exhibition: The Other and Me in God
9. Feminist Theology as Embodied Theology
10. Disability Theologies
11. Queer Theology
12. Building up *Ekklesia* Community

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Chinese Christian Thinkers
courses.description: This course is an in-depth study of the theological perspectives of several Christian thinkers in modern and contemporary China. Case studies include T.C. Chao, Watchman Nee, Y.T Wu, Wang Mingdao, K. H. Ting, etc. Special reference shall be made on the distinctive characteristics of their theological concerns, as well as their impact on Chinese Protestantism. Their contributions on Christianity indigenization and contextualization shall also be discussed.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity or MA Theological Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students are expected to
1. Understand the basic ideas held by the selected Christian thinkers.
2. Be able to analyse, discuss and evaluate the evolution and characteristics of Protestant theological thoughts in China.
3. Demonstrate their abilities to critically reflect on and evaluate the application of the theological perspectives in China by those thinkers.
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: History, Practice, and Theology of Christian Worship
courses.description: The course is designed to provide students with an in depth study of Christian Worship from Biblical, historical, liturgical, theological and contextual perspectives. After laying the foundation for liturgical and theological discussions from Biblical and historical angles, much emphasis will be placed on the development of worship forms from Vatican II to the recent ecumenical and post denominational liturgical revivals that reflect dynamic contemporary cultural and theological dialogues in the post modern era.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity, MA in Theological Studies, MA in Christian Studies, MA in Religious Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge outcome:
The students should have a solid historical sketch of the development of various traditions of Christian worship.
Attitude outcome:
The students may cultivate an ecumenical mind and become more appreciative of other traditions different from their own.
Skill outcome:
The students are able to make use other traditions to enhance their own in the evaluation and conduct of Christian worship.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Christian Worship and The Spirit of Liturgy
2. Biblical Basis of Christian Worship: Worship in Truth and Spirit (John 4: 19-24);Worship As Dialogue (Isaiah 6: 1-8); Design and Discharge of Worship (1 Corinthians 14).
3. The Language of Time: Church Calendar and Lectionary of the Christian Year.
4. Daily Office; Composition of Corporate Prayers.
5. The Language of Space: The Function of Liturgical Space; History of Liturgical Architecture; Liturgical Art
6. Symbols and Rituals in Christian Worship.
7. The Liturgy of the Primitive Church vis-à-vis Gnosticism and Paganism
8. The Sacraments and Christian Initiation
9. The Eucharist: The Shape and Theology of the West and the East Rites.
10. Reformation and Liturgical Reforms: The Normative Principle and Regulative Principle; The Anglican, Lutheran and Reformed Traditions; The Non-conformists: Quakers, Free Church, and Charismatic.
11. Liturgical Renewal of Vatican II and Ecumenical Movement
12. Sacred Music and Worship
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Models of Practical Theology
courses.description: This course aims at familiarizing the students with the practical theology movement in the past several decades. It will examine the practical nature of all theologies, and will introduce several models of practical theology. It also aims at helping students to see how the theological theories that they learn through lectures and readings may have bearings on their Christian lives and ministries.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity or MA Theological Studies
courses.course_syllabus:
What is Practical Theology?
- Nature of Theology—Theoretical or Practical or “theoretical vs. practical”?
- Duns Scotus and the debate over the nature of Theology in the Thirteenth/Fourteenth Century
- Practical Theology as a discipline—historical development
- Types/ Models/ Paradigms of Practical Theology
- On Practical Theology in Chinese Speaking Societies
- Methods and methodologies of Practical Theology
- --Empirical (qualitative inquiry) approach
- ----the approaches widespread in the British circles
- ----Illustrations
- -------A research on Protestant Death rites
- -------Spiritual Care in multifaith settings
- --Practical Theology as Action Research
- --Hermeneutical Approach
- ----theory and practice, application
- ----What is “Practical”/”Practice”?
- ----“Application” and Understanding: the Fundamental Hermeneutic Problem
- ----Illustration: Wesleyan reflection on Pathological Gambling
- --Stephen Pattison’s Practical Theology as “Critical Conversation”
- --Practical Theology as Critical Social Theory
- ----Illustrations:
- -------Lutheran reflection on local Higher Education in the context of Economic Globalization
- -------Church Growth discourse (HK)
- -------WHO spirituality vs. Asian Spirituality
- ----Class Experiment: *enjo kosai*

Some Domains (examples) of Practical Theology:
- Theological Education
- Theological Reflection
- --Models of theological reflection
- --Disjuncture and theological reflection
- --Learning style and theological reflection
- ----Reflection via integrative seminar

Integrative Seminar x 4:
- Students’ presentation (no audit [except special students] is allowed)
- by random assignment: 8 presenters + 8 reflection partners (2, 2, 2, 2)
- Each reflection partner group consists of two students who will engage in pre-session reflection with the two presenters separately.
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: The Reformation Era
courses.description: The 16th century brought a profound paradigm shift in the development of Christianity that has fundamentally changed church, society, and culture in the West. This change has had a global impact and played a crucial role in the process of modernization. The course introduces the students to the developments in church, theology, and society in 16th century Europe with a particular emphasis on the deep theological changes, particularly those connected to Luther, Calvin, and the Radical Reformation.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Students shall be able to systematically and coherently understand different aspects of the transformations happening during this period: theological, spiritual, historical, social, political, and others.
• Students will extend their knowledge to how shifts in theological thinking affected the traditional configuration of society, state, culture, and religion
• The students will develop skills to make appropriate judgments about different perspectives on church history and issues that are still debated.
• The students will develop sensitivity regarding the diversity of Christian faith expressions.
• The students will learn to apply theological concepts based on the theoretical paradigms of the Reformation to assess controversial issues of the present.
courses.course_syllabus:
• Political, social, and cultural context of the late medieval time
• Medieval theology as background to the theological debates of the Reformation
• Historical aspects of the main reformers Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin and of the Reformation in England
• Systematic theological aspects of Reformation thought: o Soteriology
o Sacraments
o Ecclesiology
o Political theology
• Historical aspects of the post-Reformation period
• Reforms in Roman Catholicism
• Ecclesial, cultural, social, and political impacts of the Reformation
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Modern Western Christianity
courses.description: The purpose of the course is to introduce the students to the historical and theological developments in the Western Church from the Peace of Westphalia through Enlightenment, the history of awakenings and the renewals in the 20th century to the present. This course includes both developments of the church in Europe and North America, as they are closely linked.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
• The students will extend their knowledge of theological and ecclesial developments during the period.
• The students will be able to critically evaluate how, during the studied period, religious institutions influenced socio‐political developments and vice versa.
• The students will develop skills to make appropriate judgments about different perspectives on church history and issues that are still debated.
• The students will develop sensitivity regarding the diversity of Christian faith expressions and gain historical depth in their theological reflection.
• The critical study of church history helps the students to recover the voices of those who have been condemned as heresy.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Review: The Church during the Reformation Era; Introduction: What Moves Church History? The Church at the Beginning of Modernity
2. The Roman-Catholic Church during the 17th and 18th Centuries: Tradition and Revivalism
3. Faith vs Reason: The Church during the Period of Enlightenment I
4. Faith vs Reason: The Church during the Period of Enlightenment II
5. Church and Politics: Puritanism; Spiritual Movements in 17th and 18th Century Protestantism: Pietism and Methodism
6. Protestant Revival in the 18th and 19th Centuries: The First and Second Great Awakening
7. Revivalism in the 19th and 20th Centuries: Holiness Movement, Divine Healing and the Rise of Modern Pentecostalism and Charismatic Christianity
8. Tradition and Modernity: Roman Catholicism in the 19th and 20th Centuries
9. Protestantism in the 19th and 20th Centuries: Responding to Social Issues
10. The Church and Totalitarian Ideologies: Protestantism during the Wartime (Film-Watching)
11. Renewal in the 20th Century: Ecumenism and Evangelicalism
12. Christianity as A World Religion
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Biblical Hebrew I
courses.description: This course, and the sequel Biblical Hebrew II in the next semester, are designed to enable students to read Biblical Hebrew. In this course, Biblical Hebrew I, students learn the alphabets to the basic forms of Hebrew sentences. Students not only learn how to read simple sentences from the Hebrew bible, but also learn to identify different parts of speech, and basic grammar. Students will also learn some Hebrew songs which accompany the lessons. This course follows closely to its textbook, Learn Biblical Hebrew by John H. Dobson (2005). Biblical Hebrew I will cover Lessons 1-13.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity and MA in Theological Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes
(1) recite and write down from memory the Hebrew alphabets, vowels and their transliterations
(2) pronounce and read Hebrew words
(3) recite from memory Genesis 1:1 (D 2.4; p. 18); Deuteronomy 6:4-5 (D 5.6; p. 55); the songs: We welcome you (D 1.13 Q5; p. 16) and Blessed are You (D 5.9 Q6; p. 58)
(4) memorize at least 350 Hebrew words perfectly by the end of the course
(5) recognize words and identify them correctly as nouns, verbs, prepositions, constructs, suffixes, adjectives, infinitives or participles
(6) identify the forms of questions, commands and requests
(7) parse a given word
(8) explain the usage of adjectives, participles, infinitives, prefix and suffix conjugations, waw consecutive conjugation as well as concepts of perfective and non-perfective
(9) deduce the functions of each component after parsing a given sentence
(10) identify basic grammar implications in simple Hebrew sentences or phrases

Attitude Outcomes
(1) develop an interest and respect for the historical and cultural development of the Hebrew language from its paleo-Hebrew script until its Aramaic script, and the modern Hebrew language
(2) appreciate the distinctiveness of the Biblical Hebrew language
(3) cultivate an interest to read Biblical Hebrew texts
courses.course_syllabus:
1. The Hebrew Alphabets and Vowels
2. Word Order in Sentences
3. The Pronominal Suffixes and Pronouns
4. The Narrative and Completed Action
5. Parsing
6. The Adjectives
7. Absolute and Construct Nouns
8. The Continuing Action
9. The Previous and Future Action
10. Possession and Question Tags
11. Commands and Requests
12. Infinitives
13. Numbers

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Biblical Hebrew II
courses.description: This course, a sequel to Biblical Hebrew I, will continue to follow the textbook, Learn Biblical Hebrew by John H. Dobson (2005), covering Lessons 12–25. It will cover all the binyanim of Hebrew as well as understanding concepts of Hebrew syntax, function of prepositions and the principles of translating narratives and poetry and attempt a few exercises. In particular, we shall read the Masoretic text of the book of Jonah (a narrative with a poem) with the help of the Lexicons/Dictionaries and other Bible aids.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in Master of Divinity and MA in Theological Studies
Pre-requisite: Hebrew I (THEO1213 or THEO3217 or THEO5301)
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes

The students will be competent in the following abilities:

(a) recognize every component in the parts of speech learned in THEO5301

(b) identify the binyanim and functions of all verbs

(c) recall the forms and functions of the prepositions and particles

(d) identify, recognize at least 500 of the most common Biblical Hebrew words found in the Hebrew Bible

(e) search words in the Biblical Hebrew dictionaries and lexicons and explain the entries, in particular the BDB Lexicon.

(f) parse and translate given phrases/sentences and the book of Jonah

(g) use the parsing tools of Bible Works 10

(h) read and translate short narrative passages and some poems from the Hebrew Bible

(i) read and explain the grammar in the book of Jonah

Attitude Outcomes

The students will:

(a) be confident to read a Biblical Hebrew passage on their own with the necessary tools

(b) develop the habit of reading Biblical Hebrew passages

(c) appreciate the basic tasks to do exegesis and interpretation

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: New Testament Greek I
courses.description: This course provides students with an introduction to the basic grammar and vocabulary of New Testament Greek, in order to enable students to read the original New Testament texts.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity and MA in Theological Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:
On the successful completion of this unit, students should be able to:
1. master the basic syntax and a working vocabulary of New Testament Greek; and
2. read and translate simple Greek texts

Attitude Outcomes:
Throughout the learning process, students are expected to:
1. develop a regular revision practice;
2. develop a positive attitude to face difficulties in learning; and
3. develop an initiative to help others and seek help from others by means of group study.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Pronunciation of Greek words:
- Sound and rules of pronunciation of alphabet
- Rules on accent and syllables
2. Bible Reading and Analysis
- Listening and reading Matthew 6 and John 1
3. Noun
- Concept of declension; first and second declension
- Pronouns: personal and demonstrative pronouns
- Basic modifier of noun
4. Greek Verb System
- Concept of inflection, mood, tense, aspect and voice
- Present and future indicative
- Imperfect and aorist active indicative
5. Preposition
- Basic rules on the use of most commonly used prepositions
courses.feedback_evaluation:

courses.description: This course is a continuation of New Testament Greek I. It provides students with an introduction to the essential elements to New Testament Greek. Students will master different aspects of Greek morphology and syntax and acquire a substantial reading vocabulary. In order to enhance learning, the course employs both deductive and inductive methods.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Introduction to the Hebrew Bible
courses.description: This course orientates students to the diverse scholarship which encompasses the study of the Hebrew Scripture: from archaeology, historical-critical, grammatico-historical, socio-historical methodologies to the history of composition of the biblical books, languages, religions and literature of the period before the common era. Inevitably, it also introduces the world of the ancient Near East – its history, religions and literature, which the Hebrew Scripture belonged and related to. This course traces the challenges confronted bythe nation of Israel from its beginning up until the period of the Second Temple.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in Master of Divinity
Exclusion: THEO5919 The Hebrew Bible in Contexts
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:
1. The students will know and understand
a. the general overview of the contents in the Hebrew Bible
b. the direct relationship of the composition of the books to her contexts
c. a general grasp of the scholarship pertaining to the study of the Hebrew Bible
2. The students can describe, explain and discuss
a. the main issues related to the composition and redaction of the books in the Hebrew Bible
b. the main issues of critical scholarship concerning the origin and identity of Israel
c. the proposed historical contexts of the Hebrew Bible
d. the relationships or/and tensions between the traditions underlying the theological motivations and the contemporary
e. situation/s of the text

Attitude Outcomes:
The students will appreciate
a. the making/compilation of the Hebrew Bible
b. the necessity for language acquisition in the study of the Hebrew Bible
c. the diverse research faculties in the study of the Hebrew Bible
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction: Course Introduction; Introduction: Imaginative Remembering; Literature and Genre
2. Torah (1): Introduction to Torah Hebrew Bible as (Christian) Scripture
3. Torah (2): Genesis; Exodus 1-18 Myth, Legend and ANET/Archaeology
4. Torah (3): Exodus 25-40, Leviticus, Number 1-10; Cult and Priestly school
5. Torah (4): Exodus 19-24, Numbers 11-36, Deuteronomy; Law and Narrative
6. Prophets (1): Introduction to the Prophets, Joshua, Judges; History and Deuteronomistic History
7. Prophets (2): Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel; Literary Prophet and Their Social World
8. Prophets (3): 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings; Narrative and Ideology
9. Prophets (4): Minor Prophets; Twelve prophet as a book

11. Writings (2): Job, Proverbs; Wisdom Literature
12. Writings (3): Five Scrolls, Ezra-Nehemiah; Hebrew Bible and the early Judaism
13. Writings (4)/ Conclusion: Daniel, 1 and 2 Chronicles; Apocalyptic Literature and the Rewritten Bible; Concluding Reflection: Hiddenness of God

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Introduction to the New Testament
courses.description: The main purpose of this course is to give students a general understanding the text of the New Testament, its methods of studies, its background and the issues involved. To achieve this purpose, it is necessary for students to know how the NT is interpreted in the light of modern thoughts. This involves firstly a good knowledge of the meaning of the basic text of the NT - this is in fact the prerequisite condition for students who are going to take this course; those do not know the text of the NT have to read through it twice (both students who are going to take this course; those do not know the text of the NT have to read through it twice (both Chinese and English version) at least. Besides, students are also required to read some basic works of modern interpretation of the NT.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in Master of Divinity
Exclusion THEO5910 New Testament in Contexts
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:
1. To give students a general understanding the text of the New Testament, its methods of studies, its background and the issues involved; and
2. To be able to grasp the method of Bible study and exegesis, particularly Pauline Letters.
Skills Outcomes:
1. To enhance critical intelligence thinking; and
2. To enhance analytical ability throughout exegesis.
Attitude Outcomes
1. To develop one’s ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of different church traditions and scholarly perspectives; and
2. To develop one’s sensitivity to the limit of doctrines and enhance openness to different exegesis.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. History of the New Testament
- Investigate the emergence of New Testament and how it became a cannon of Christianity.
2. Contexts of New Testament
- Investigate the social, political, economic, philosophical and literary context of New Testament and how they affect the development of the text.
3. New Testament Criticisms
- Investigate the basic ideas and methodology of major historical criticisms of New Testament
4. Interpretation of New Testament
- Basic interpretation method in interpreting New Testament in light of the contexts
5. Main theme of different books
- Introducing the basic thoughts of various books in New Testament

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Synoptic Gospels
courses.description: This course comprises a study of the purpose and theology of the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark and Luke), comparing their distinct characteristics and looking at their similarities and differences. The course begins with a critical survey of the history of the Synoptic problem (how to explain the relationship between Matthew, Mark, and Luke) and proposed solutions. Exegesis of selected passages will be carried out to understand the original setting of individual gospel.

Attitude Outcomes:

2. To develop one’s sensitivity to the limit of doctrines and enhance openness to different exegesis.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Pauline Letters
courses.description: This course is a study of the Pauline and Deuteropauline Letters. Through comparing some of the critical passages from both categories, the course will explore the dating, authorship, purpose and the development of the Pauline theology.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:
1. To have basic knowledge of the content, theology and historical context of Pauline Letters;
2. To have basic knowledge of historical Paul;
3. To be able to understand particularly the first letter of Pauline Letters (i.e. the Letter to the Romans); and
4. To be able to grasp the method of Bible study and exegesis, particularly Pauline Letters.

Skills Outcomes:
1. To enhance critical intelligence thinking; and
2. To enhance analytical ability throughout exegesis.

Attitude Outcomes:
1. To develop one’s ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of different church traditions and scholarly perspectives; and
2. To develop one’s sensitivity to the limit of doctrines and enhance openness to different exegesis.

1. Course Introduction + Problems in interpreting Paul
2. Basic concept in interpreting Pauline letters
3. Interpretation history of Pauline letters
4. Context of Paul (1): 2nd temple Judaism and New Perspective of Paul
5. Context of Paul (2): Social World of Paul including the Political and Economic situation of Roman Empire
6. Core Pauline theological motif 1 - Theology
7. Core Pauline theological motif 2 – Eschatology
8. Core Pauline theological motif 3 - Christology
9. Core Pauline theological motif 4 - Love
10. Interpretation Method: Socio-rhetorical Interpretation 2
11. Letter to Philemon: Demonstration of SRI application
12. Conclusion

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Pentateuchal Studies
courses.description: This course covers the major scholarship pertaining to the books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. It not only examines the themes and historical purposes for these books, but also orientates the students to the complexities of the contents and purposes for these books as evidenced by the prominent scholarship throughout the 19th to the 21st century. It tracks the recent development of the debates pertaining to the source theories of J, E, D and P; and also recent alternative theories and methodologies to the study of the Pentateuch.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:
The students will know and understand:
a. the general influence of the ancient Near East cultures on the composition of the Pentateuch
b. the scholarship on Pentateuch in relation to the composition, history, themes and methodologies of interpretations from 19th – 21st century
c. the source theories of J, E, D and P.
The students can describe, explain and discuss and evaluate
a. the themes and purposes of the Pentateuch
b. the historical and social contexts of the Pentateuch
c. the relationship of the Pentateuch to the rest of the Hebrew Bible
d. the contemporary scholarship emerging in Pentateuchal scholarship with regards to methodologies of interpretation
e. the current status of J, E, D and P.

Attitude Outcomes:
The students will appreciate:
a. the process of the composition, redaction and transmission of the Pentateuch
b. the significance of Pentateuch to the Jews and its continual influence on the three communities of faith: Judaism, Islam and Christianity
courses.course_syllabus:
Week1:
1. Syllabus
2. Introduction to the Pentateuch: Current Theories and Core Issues

Week2:
The Pentateuch and the Ancient Southwest Asian Texts

Week3:
The Formation of the Pentateuch
1. Documentary Hypothesis
2. Alternative approaches
3. Priestly and Non‐Priestly
4. Exilic Yahwist as the author/redactor/historian

Week4:
Pentateuch, Tetrateuch, Hexateuch, or Enneateuch?

Week5:
Current Theories:
1. Persian Authorization of the Torah
2. The Persian/Hellenistic Origins of the “Biblical Historiography”

Week6:
Genesis:
1. Creation and Priestly Genealogy
2. The Patriarchal Stories

Week7:
Exodus:
1. The Exodus Story
2. The Law Codes: The Covenant Code, Deuteronomic Code, Holiness Code

Week8:
Leviticus: Priestly Cosmology

Week9:
Numbers: In the Wilderness

Week10:
Deuteronomy:
1. Deuteronomy and Ancient Vassal Treaties
2. Deuteronomy as Constitution

Week11:
Newer Exegetical Lens:
1. Socioeconomic Class
2. Gender and Sexuality

Week12:
Newer Exegetical Lens:
1. Race and Ethnicity
2. Cross‐Textual Criticism
Concluding Remarks
1. What was/is the Pentateuch? Law, History, or Scripture
2. Ethics of Interpretation

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Prophetic Literature
courses.description: This course covers selected readings from the second portion of the Hebrew bible, the Prophets, in particular the latter prophets, which includes Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the book of the Twelve (Minor Prophets). Historical studies aided with contextual interpretations will be the approach taken in engaging the biblical text, while theological and exegetical studies of the text will interact vigorously with contemporary social, political, economic and cultural dimensions of the public life. Insights and influences from modern literary and critical theories, social sciences and humanities, and various inter-disciplinary approaches will also be introduced and applied in the course of interpretation.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
Knowledge Outcomes:
(1) To be able to understand prophetic literature in terms of its historical scholarship and contemporary interpretations.
(2) To be able to engage the prophetic text with contemporary contextual issues.
Attitude Outcomes
(1) To develop students’ ability to have a critical and yet sympathetic understanding and appreciation of the prophetic literature of
the Hebrew bible within the milieu of modern biblical scholarship.
(2) To develop students’ sensitivity to the relevancy of biblical prophetic literature to the public dimension of human life.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. The social world of the Hebrew prophets: This section covers the role of a prophet and the nature of prophecy in ancient Southwest Asia and Israel in relation to the social issues of its time.
2. The historical context: The Hebrew prophets will be situated in their signifying contexts from the Neo-Assyrian empire to the Persian empire.
3. Major sections and Individual books: The structure and literary features of prophetic literature of different major sections (the Former Prophets, the Latter Prophets, and the Twelve) and individual books will be adumbrated.
4. Critical approaches: Recent scholarship in a variety of critical methods will be discussed.
5. Theological notions: Major theological notions include covenant, messianism, inviolability of Zion, theodicy, retributive logic, universalism, ḥesed, and restoration.
6. Critical issues: Critical issues include vaticinium ex eventu, the scheme of prophecy and fulfillment, social justice, the marital and sexual metaphor, divine violence, and historicity.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Early and Medieval Church
courses.description: The purpose of the course is to introduce the students to the historical and theological developments in the early and medieval church, from Jesus to the dawn of the Reformation and to engage them in a critical dialogue with earlier forms of contextualization of the Christian faith.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
a) The students will gain a general knowledge of the theological and ecclesial development during the covered period.
b) The students become familiar with key doctrinal development and the interplay between religious institutions and socio-political circumstances of the early and medieval period of the church.
c) The students will get acquainted with different perspectives on church history and with issues that are still debated.
d) The students will develop sensitivity regarding the diversity of Christian faith expressions and gain historical depth in their theological reflection.
e) The students learn about historical forms of contextualization.
f) The critical study of church history helps the students to recover the voices of those who have been condemned as heresy.
courses.course_syllabus:
Session 1:
Introduction to the course
The church in the first two centuries
• What is the Relation of Jesus to the Church?
• Steps in the Development of the Early Church and the spread of Christianity
• The Separation between the Church and the Jewish Community

Session 2: Christianity and politics
Conflicts with the State
The extension of Christianity in the first three centuries

Session 3: Challenges to the faith in the second century and the development of early Catholic theology
The pre-catholic church
Gnostic crisis, Marcionism and the Montanist crisis
Response to the challenges to the faith: Development of catholic theology

Session 4: Christianity and culture: The encounter with Hellenist philosophy
Hellenistic philosophies
Patristic theology
The early Trinitarian debates

Session 5: Christianity becoming the religion of the empire
The so-called Constantinian conversion
Religious policy after Constantine
Constantine’s impact on the religious life of the catholic church
Impact on the theology of the catholic church
Counter-movements to the imperial church: Ascetism and monasticism

Session 6: Theological and ecclesial controversies of the 4th century
Donatism
The Arian controversy until the Council of Nicea
The continuation of the controversy until Constantinople

Session 7: Theology and christological debates in the 5th century
The Council of Chalcedon
Augustine

Session 8: Mission history: the extension of Christianity and its inculturation in new contexts
The Encounter of the catholic church with non-Roman kingdoms
Shifts in world Christianity and the confrontation with Islam

Session 9: Church and state: The growth of papal and ecclesial power
The history of the papal claim of primacy
The development of the secular power of the popes
The conflict between the papacy and the Empire
Medieval papacy, church and state

Session 10: The history of a growing division: The churches in East and West on separate ways
Christological debates of the 6th and 7th century
The iconoclastic debate

Session 11: The history of the other church: Revivalism, reform, and alternative
Christian faith expression in medieval times
Christian mysticism
Monastic reform movements
Mendicant orders
Radical and heretical movements
The Catholic Church and the ‘other church’

Session 12: Outward militancy and inward divisions in high and late medieval times
The crusades
The inquisition
The Babylonian captivity of the church and the divided papacy
The conciliar church reform movement

Session 13: Theological Developments during the Medieval Time
Representatives, forms and historical development of medieval theology
The controversy about the universals
The controversy between rationalism and voluntarism

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: History of Christianity in Hong Kong
courses.description: This course aims at helping students to gain a comprehensive understanding on the history of Protestant Christianity in Hong Kong. The first section will emphasize on the historical development of Christianity in different stages. The second section will investigate the relationship and interaction between Christianity and Hong Kong society from topical perspectives.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
Learning outcomes
(1) To assist students to understand the historical development of Christianity in Hong Kong.
(2) To assist students to acquaint the methods of conducting research on local church history
Attitude Outcomes
(1) To develop and affirm students’ identity towards local church history
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction: A Macro-history of Christianity in Hong Kong
2. Founding and Pioneering: The Initiation of Hong Kong Christianity (1841 - 1860)
3. South China and Hong Kong: Development and Self-governance (1860 - 1936)
4. Immigrants and Gospel (1937 - 1960s)
5. The Formation of Localized Churches (1970s - )
6. Mission and Education: A History of Church-run Schools in Hong Kong
7. Heaven and Society: Christianity and Social Engagement
8. God and Caesar: Church-State Relations in Hong Kong
9. Gospel and Culture: A Fusion of the West, East, and Local

courses.description: This course introduces both the historical and theological development of Christian doctrine of humanity and salvation.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To acquire the basic knowledge of Christian doctrine of humanity and salvation.
2. To gain an integrated theological perspective and methodology so that students can be critically engaged in theological construction.
3. To have a positive commitment to human welfare.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Systematic Theology I
courses.description: Systematic theology can be understood as the theological discipline that constructively articulates the meaning, coherence, and implications of Christian beliefs. This course aims at providing students with a solid methodological foundation for the study of systematic theology by investigating various issues that belong to the “prolegomena” of systematic theology, including the formative factors of theology (such as revelation, Bible, tradition, experience, reason, and culture), theological language, and theological methods.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes: After completing this course, the student is expected (a) to have an historical overview of the major paradigms in Christian theology; (b) to understand significant issues and diverse views regarding the formative factors of theology (especially the Bible, but also tradition, culture, theological language, etc.); (c) to have basic knowledge of exemplary theological systems and methods; (d) to be able to think analytically and critically in the field of theology.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. What Is Systematic Theology?
2. Emergence of Christian Theology in the Patristic Era
3. Medieval and Reformation Theology
4. Theology in Modernity
5. Theological Language
6. Revelation and Jesus Christ
7. Scripture (1)
8. Scripture (2)
9. Tradition
10. Experience and Reason
11. Culture and Society
12. Theological Systems and Methods (1)
13. Theological Systems and Methods (2)

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Pastoral Theology
courses.description: This course covers three areas: 1) the historical and theological position of Pastoral Theology in Theological Studies and its uniqueness; 2) different types of Pastoral Theology and their aims; and 3) Ancient and contemporary church models and pastoral emphases.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
To understand what is Pastoral Theology with reflection from personal pastoral experience.
To construct Pastoral Theology from the Bible, church and Chinese cultural traditions.
To understand different emphases of Pastoral Theology from multiple perspectives and from histories of different denominations.
courses.course_syllabus:
Session 1: The Pastor as a Person (1)—Pastor’s Relationships: The Congregation, Collegiality, Denomination and the Society.
Session 2: The Pastoral Office-The Ordination of the Ministry of Word and Sacraments.
Session 3: The Local Church-An Institutional Organization and a Living Organism.
Session 4: The Pastor as the Priest
Session 5: The Pastor as the Celebrant; Administration of Holy Baptism and Holy Communion
Session 6: The Pastor as Preacher and Teacher;
Session 7: Preaching According to the Church Calendar and Planning of the Pulpit.
Session 8: The Pastor as a Person (2)--Pastor’s Capability: Gifts, Spirituality, Attitude and Mental Hygiene.
Session 9: The Pastor as Prophet
Session 10: The Pastor as Counselor
Session 11: The Pastor as Leader and Change Agent
Session 12: Pastoral Ethics
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.description:
This course will cover: 1) the principles, construction and technique in preaching; and
2) the content and message of a sermon in contemporary world. This course will include video-taping students’ preaching. Tutorials after preaching will be conducted for the improvement of technique and content.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes:
To understand the principle of preaching on theological topics.
To understand the integration of different types of preaching and the way of preparation.
To learn and practice the techniques and styles in delivering a sermon.
courses.course_syllabus:
(一) 課程評估
分享／引論
聽道／講道經驗及心得
何謂講道學（Homiletics）？
講道的構成因素——真道、表達、使命、講者、聽眾、技巧、權柄
(二) 真道
何謂道？
聖經與道
宣講與教導之不同
道與行
(三) 講章的分類
專題式講道
經文式講道
釋經講道
(四) 講章的性質
佈道
培靈
奮興
牧養
婚禮
喪追思
紀念日
聖曆及特別主日
(五) 經文的選擇與運用
用一段經文的好處
選擇經文要留意的地方
如何運用經文
(六) 如何決定主旨
主旨的必要
主旨的選擇
(七) 如何決定題目
(八) 講章的結構
分段與大綱
引論、本論、結論
(九) 導言
三個目的
(十) 例證
講道的天窗
(十一) 結論與應用
應用的重要性
應用的三個成份
應用的動機
(十二) 講章的準備和組成的步驟
探索期
專注期
講章的組合
最後的準備
(十三) 講道的技巧
講者的素質與風格
講章的表達與演繹
(十四) 試講

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Preaching
courses.description: Through lectures, reading and self-studies, students learn how to compose and deliver sermon. Special emphasis will be given to Biblical exposition, progression of thoughts, flow of feelings, use of illustrations, relevancy, and deliver styles. Critiques, suggestions, or comments by the instructor and interaction in a small group will be facilitated. Each student is expected to deliver a full-length sermon in front of other students two to three times a semester and hand in the relevant scripts at the same time. Students need to hand in the revised scripts in two weeks’ time.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Master of Divinity
courses.learning_outcomes: Learn how to compose and deliver sermons of 30 minutes and learn how to make comments and give suggestions to sermons preached by others.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. 課程介紹；宣道者個人靈性、學養、性向與風格的關係
2. 既是宣講，也是做神學(Doing theology)：宣講、神學與處境之關聯
3. 出外觀摩
4. 宣講微技巧
5. 講章類別的撰寫與演繹：釋經講道(Expository preaching)
6. 觀摩與評論1；宣講與修辭技巧
7. 觀摩與評論2；講章類別的撰寫與演繹：主題式講道(Topical preaching)
8. 觀摩與評論3；講章類別的撰寫與演繹：處境講道(Situational preaching)
9. 觀摩與評論4；講章類別的撰寫與演繹：敘事講道(Narrative preaching)
10. 觀摩與評論5；講章類別的撰寫與演繹：佈道式講道(Evangelistic preaching)
11. 觀摩與評論6；宣講與多媒體應用
12. 觀摩與評論7；向不同群體的宣講方式
13. 觀摩與評論8；信仰立場先於政治考量的宣講
courses.feedback_evaluation: An end-of-term university-wide course evaluation will be conducted in class. Students’ comments and feedback on the course through e-mail or personal meetings with instructor and/or tutors are always welcomed.

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: Methods and Paradigms of Christian Studies
courses.description: This course aims at providing students with a solid methodological and theoretical understanding of the multidisciplinary study of Christianity. It mainly introduces the students to the principal tasks (e.g., historical, constructive, practical) and methods, together with their theoretical presuppositions, of Christian studies. It also acquaints students with major theological paradigms (e.g., traditional, liberal, liberationist, feminist, etc.) and their different visions of the theological disciplines (e.g., biblical studies, history of Christianity, systematic theology, pastoral studies, etc.). Issues such as the relation of Christian studies to other academic fields, the alleged conflict between its scientific and ecclesial orientations, and the interconnection of its diverse disciplines, will be discussed.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MA in Christian Studies and MA in Religious Studies programmes.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To obtain a broadened and deepened understanding of the major traditions of Christianity in the world in historical and comparative perspectives
2. To be able to understand major theological paradigms in Christianity with their internal complexity, and be able to extend such understanding to issues in church and society
3. To have some knowledge of the tasks and methods of the major disciplines in Christian studies and be able to apply such knowledge in research
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction. Christianity as Multi- Paradigmatic.
2. Historical-Theological Paradigms (1): Early Jewish-Christian Apocalyptic; Patristic Hellenistic Orthodox
3. Historical-Theological Paradigms (2): Mediaeval Latin Roman Catholic; Reformation Protestant.
4. Theological Research and Paper Writing
5. The Tasks and Methods of Biblical Studies
6. The Tasks and Methods of History of Christianity
7. Historical-Theological Paradigms (3): Modernity; Liberal Theology; Neo-Orthodox Theology.
8. Historical-Theological Paradigms (4): Evangelicalism; Pentecostalism
9. The Tasks and Methods of Systematic Theology
10. Historical-Theological Paradigms (5): Liberation Theology; Feminist Theology.
11. The Tasks and Methods of Practical Theology
12. Global Christianity in the 21st century
13. Interdisciplinary approaches to Christian Studies

courses.subject: THEO
courses.title: New Testament in Contexts
courses.description: This course will select some texts of the New Testament with contemporary methods for in-depth study. Texts include selected themes of the Pauline Epistles, Synoptic Gospels and Johannine Literature, e.g., Pauline Epistle Form, Doctrinal and Ethical Teachings; Eucharist, Baptism, Miracles and Teachings of the Synoptics; as well as Revelation structure, “I am saying”, Farewell Discourse of the Gospel of John.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Exclusion=Not for students who have taken THEO5312 Introduction to the New Testament
For students in MA Religious Studies or MA Christian Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing this course, students should be able to:
Expected Knowledge Outcomes
1. Know how to find reliable and trustworthy resources for their own reconstruction of socio-historical contexts of the New Testament;
2. Compare and contrast New Testament studies in public domain with uncritical voices by means of established paradigms and academic consensus;
Expected Skills Outcome
3. Analyze context(s) behind primary texts and evaluate their relevance in biblical exegeses; (\* This also serve as a preparation of key research skills for graduate work in advanced biblical studies)
Expected Attitude Outcome
4. Deepen their critical and yet sympathetic understanding of earliest Christian traditions in our contemporary contexts and appraise their contributions in shaping different cultures.
courses.course_syllabus:
• Matrix and Methods (NT as sacred text and historical source, social historical contexts of Judaism
and Greco-Roman culture in the first century, textual criticism, source criticism, form criticism,
redaction criticism, narrative criticism, sociological approach, ideology criticism, history of
effects)
• The Four Gospels (Mark, Matthew, Luke, John; literary design and social historical contexts,
Christology and discipleship)
• Paul’s Letters (Philemon, First Thessalonians, First Corinthians, Romans, Galatians; contexts and
contents; crises and messages)
• Other Writings (Pastoral Epistles, Peter’s Letters, Hebrews, Revelation; hostile contexts, church
formation in the world, hope beyond now)
